clue.text: A cat, say, can give out

indicators.note: say tells the solver to speak the phrase and listen to how it comes out

parts.note: an ounce is a cat, the snow leopard; 'a cat' is thus 'an ounce'

explanation.surface: Someone wonders whether a cat or a tin can might be thrown out.
explanation.walkthrough: The ounce is another name for the snow leopard; 'an ounce' spoken runs together into the answer. 'can' is a link word.
explanation.definitionFit: To give out news is to declare or proclaim it publicly, a straightforward synonym.

clue.text: Don't go 11 river during drink

indicators.note: during means the river sits inside the drink, in the middle of it

parts.note: to sup is to drink in sips
the Tay is the longest river in Scotland

explanation.surface: A drinker is told not to wander off down by the river while having a drink.
explanation.walkthrough: 11 is DOWN, so the definition reads 'Don't go down'. The Tay is a Scottish river.
explanation.definitionFit: Remaining aloft rather than descending is the opposite of going down; an idiomatic phrase.

clue.text: Rodent wanting tail fixed finds monkey

indicators.note: wanting its tail means the rodent's last letter is dropped

parts.note: the marmot is a burrowing rodent
set means fixed or firm

explanation.surface: A rodent with a mended tail turns out to be a monkey.
explanation.walkthrough: 'wanting tail' drops the last letter of the rodent; 'finds' is only a link between wordplay and definition.
explanation.definitionFit: The marmoset is a small South American primate, a kind of monkey.

clue.text: Wanted to find variety on the radio

indicators.note: on the radio means heard rather than seen, so the word is judged by its sound

parts.note: a sort is a kind or variety

explanation.surface: Someone wished to come across a variety show broadcast on the radio.
explanation.walkthrough: In a non-rhotic British accent the word for a kind sounds just like the answer; 'to find' is a link.
explanation.definitionFit: Sought is the past tense of seek, meaning looked for or desired.

clue.text: Little more than a few 19s

definitions.meaning: 19 is SECOND; sixty seconds make this unit of time, rather more than a few

explanation.surface: Something is only slightly more than a handful of seconds.
explanation.definitionFit: The adjective (stress on the second syllable) means tiny, while the noun is sixty seconds.

clue.text: Fawning type showing bit of leg?

parts.note: a mini is a skirt that shows a bit of leg
on means showing, as a film is on at the cinema

explanation.surface: A sycophant is the sort to flash a little leg to win favour.
explanation.walkthrough: Read the answer as 'mini on': wearing a miniskirt is showing a bit of leg.
explanation.definitionFit: A minion is a servile follower or underling, a fawning hanger-on.

clue.text: Little jumper lining piece that's coloured

indicators.note: lining means the jumper goes inside, the way a lining sits within a coat

parts.note: a man is a piece in chess or draughts
roo is short for kangaroo, a jumper in more ways than one

explanation.surface: A small knitted jumper has a lining in a coloured piece of cloth.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Little jumper' is not a sweater but a shortened kangaroo, ROO; 'that's' is a link.
explanation.definitionFit: Maroon is a dark brownish-red, so describing something as that shade calls it coloured.

clue.text: Fool finds himself after half 9

indicators.note: after places the fool's own word behind the half-number
half means only the first two of the number's four letters are kept

parts.note: 9 written as a word is nine
himself is another fool, a twit, the fool finding his own kind

explanation.surface: A fool discovers who he really is after half past nine.
explanation.walkthrough: 'half 9' looks like a time but means half of NINE, giving NI; the fool 'himself' is another TWIT.
explanation.definitionFit: A nitwit is a silly, stupid person, a direct synonym for a fool.

clue.text: One's hired to step in after reshuffle as Foreign Secretary, for example

parts.note: a cab is something one hires for a journey

indicators.note: after reshuffle tells the solver the following words are shuffled into a new order

explanation.surface: A new appointee steps in following a Cabinet reshuffle as Foreign Secretary.
explanation.walkthrough: 'after reshuffle' signals the rearrangement of the three words that follow the hired vehicle; a cab is a hire car, and 'as' is a link.
explanation.definitionFit: The Foreign Secretary holds one of the senior ministerial jobs in the British government's top team, an example of the role.

clue.text: 10 God isn't!

definitions.meaning: 10 is ALMIGHTY, as in an almighty or dreadful row
God is never sinful or impious, so not sacred

explanation.surface: A remark that the Almighty is anything but holy.
explanation.walkthrough: 'An unholy mess' and 'an almighty mess' mean the same: dreadful, awful.
explanation.definitionFit: Unholy, informally, means dreadful or outrageous, while literally it means impious, which God is not.

clue.text: God is great

definitions.meaning: a title of the deity, the all-powerful one
informally, very big or severe, as an enormous row

explanation.surface: A simple declaration of faith: God is great.
explanation.definitionFit: The Almighty is a title for the deity, and almighty informally means tremendous.

clue.text: See 22
Opiate isn't in the wrong flower

indicators.note: in the wrong means the letters are out of their correct order

explanation.surface: Someone protests that an opiate is not to blame for a misdemeanour.
explanation.walkthrough: 'in the wrong' rearranges OPIATE ISNT.
explanation.definitionFit: The poinsettia is a Christmas plant prized for its red bracts, usually called a flower.

clue.text: Savage devastation of heartland by Newcastle area

parts.note: Newcastle is in the north-east of England, NE

indicators.note: devastation of means the following word is wrecked and rebuilt

explanation.surface: A brute wreaks havoc on the heartland near Newcastle.
explanation.walkthrough: 'devastation of' signals the anagram; NE stands for the north-east of England, where Newcastle is, and 'by' is a link.
explanation.definitionFit: Neanderthal is used as an insult for a primitive, uncivilised brute, a savage.

clue.text: Abnormal growth on sample requiring treatment

indicators.note: requiring treatment suggests the letters need working on and rearranging

explanation.surface: A tumour turns up in a biopsy sample that needs medical treatment.
explanation.walkthrough: 'requiring treatment' rearranges ON SAMPLE.
explanation.definitionFit: A neoplasm is the medical term for a tumour, new tissue growing abnormally.

clue.text: A builder of body, heavenly one

parts.note: anabolic steroids are used by bodybuilders to build muscle

explanation.surface: A bodybuilder is described as some sort of heavenly creature.
explanation.definitionFit: An asteroid is a minor planet, a body in the heavens.

clue.text: Sixties' scooter rider claiming one dropped trousers

indicators.note: claiming means taking hold of, so one sits inside the rider

parts.note: Mods were a 1960s British youth subculture who rode Vespa and Lambretta scooters

explanation.surface: A 1960s scooter rider asserts that someone pulled down his trousers.
explanation.walkthrough: Mods were British 1960s youths famous for their scooters.
explanation.definitionFit: To moon is to bare one's buttocks as a prank, which means dropping one's trousers.

clue.text: Best time in two years, given head surgery

indicators.note: surgery means the letters are cut about and rearranged

parts.note: Y is the abbreviation for year, so two years give YY

explanation.surface: Someone's prime came during a two-year period after brain surgery.
explanation.walkthrough: 'surgery' operates on HEAD plus YY together to make the answer.
explanation.definitionFit: A heyday is the period of greatest success or vigour, someone's prime.

clue.text: It's sweet to spit on goalie

parts.note: gob is British slang for spit
a goalkeeper is a shot-stopper

explanation.surface: A player thinks spitting on the goalkeeper is a lovely idea.
explanation.walkthrough: A gobstopper is a large hard round sweet, British; 'It's', 'to' and 'on' are links.
explanation.definitionFit: A gobstopper is a large hard round boiled candy, so it is a kind of confection.

clue.text: Silverback?

parts.note: split the word: silver is the medal for coming in behind the winner, and back means support a motion, which is the same word

explanation.surface: A one-word clue naming a mature male gorilla.
explanation.walkthrough: The gorilla is a red herring: split it into 'silver' and 'back', each a sense of the answer.
explanation.definitionFit: A runner-up takes silver, and to support a proposal is to endorse it in the same word.

clue.text: Six-footer, Irish, lifted tool

indicators.note: lifted means raised up, and in a down entry the letters run upwards

parts.note: an insect has six legs, so a wasp is a six-footer

explanation.surface: A tall Irishman is helped up with a tool.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Six-footer' is not a tall man but an insect with six legs; 'lifted' turns WASPIR upward in this down entry.
explanation.definitionFit: A ripsaw is a saw for cutting wood along the grain, a carpenter's tool.

clue.text: See 25
Is diligent as a 13?

definitions.meaning: 13 is NEANDERTHAL; a stooping caveman walks with his hands trailing on the ground

explanation.surface: A question whether hard work is just caveman behaviour.
explanation.definitionFit: The phrasal verb means to set to work in earnest, and literally describes knuckle-walking.

clue.text: Stick in money for imitation

indicators.note: in means the stick is placed inside the money

parts.note: pay means wages, money
a rod is a stick

explanation.surface: Someone is told to put money into a fake.
explanation.walkthrough: 'in' puts the stick inside the money, splitting it after its second letter.
explanation.definitionFit: A parody is a mocking imitation of a work's style.

clue.text: European was obliged to admit crime? On the contrary

indicators.note: on the contrary means the result runs the opposite way, read back to front
to admit means to let in, so the crime goes inside

parts.note: had, as in had to, means was obliged
a sin is a wrongdoing, loosely a crime

explanation.surface: A European was forced to own up to a crime, or so the story goes the other way.
explanation.walkthrough: 'to admit' puts the crime inside the obligation word, and 'On the contrary' reverses the result: the surface suggests contradiction, not reading backwards.
explanation.definitionFit: A Dane, someone from Denmark, is described by this adjective, so it names a European.

clue.text: Elder relatives?

parts.note: elder is a shrub or small ..., and a chart of one's relations is drawn as a branching plant

explanation.surface: A question about older members of the clan.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Elder' looks like older kin, but it is the tree; the chart of relations is the answer.
explanation.definitionFit: A genealogical diagram of ancestors branches like a plant, and elder is a plant.
